## Scope

Capable DR infrastructure (Books 01–10) does not satisfy CP-2 — **only a
signed, distributed, tested Contingency Plan document does**. The book
assembles the series' technical capabilities into a NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1
seven-section plan, anchored by a Business Impact Analysis, and closes the
full CP family (CP-2 through CP-10) with testing and after-action
artifacts.

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish a DR runbook (the middle of a response) from a CP-2
  Contingency Plan (activation, notification, sequencing, reconstitution)
  and explain why assessors write High findings absent the document.
- Conduct a BIA producing MTD, RTO, RPO, and WRT per system via
  mission-owner interviews, transaction-rate analysis, and dependency
  mapping.
- Author all seven NIST SP 800-34 sections, including activation
  thresholds, a timed notification procedure, recovery priority ordering,
  and reconstitution/failback.
- Document CP-6 alternate storage across structured data (SQL AG async
  replica), unstructured data (M365 multi-geo), application binaries, and
  IaC/policy baselines.
- Document CP-7 alternate processing (secondary cloud region,
  tested-not-designed RTOs) and CP-8 telecom redundancy (SD-WAN MPLS + DIA
  dual underlay).
- Plan and facilitate a CP-4 tabletop exercise with injects, metrics, and
  a signed After-Action Report.

## Key concepts

- "Technology without a plan fails CP-2" — the plan as artifact, not
  capability.
- BIA quartet: MTD > RTO; RTO + WRT < MTD; RPO as concrete transaction
  loss at peak.
- Five recovery phases: Activation → Notification → Recovery → Validation
  → Reconstitution.
- Contingency Plan Coordinator (CPC) authority model with named alternate.
- Dependency-driven recovery priority: network/DDI first, identity second,
  mission apps next.
- CP-6(1)/CP-7(1) geographic separation: different region, not just
  availability zone.
- Three-year test cycle: tabletop → functional failover → full recovery
  test.

## Implementation sequence

1. Inventory systems from the Book 05 SQL estate and Book 01 DDI
   dependency maps; scope the BIA.
2. Run stakeholder interviews and transaction analysis; compile the BIA
   table with mission-owner sign-off.
3. Author the seven-section plan, referencing Books 01–10 runbooks as
   appendices rather than duplicating them.
4. Document and validate CP-6 alternate storage (annual restore test) and
   CP-7 alternate processing (tested failover RTOs).
5. Document CP-8 circuit inventory, failover thresholds,
   priority-of-service provisions.
6. Execute the tabletop with deliberate injects; record metrics.
7. Produce the signed AAR; plan updates within 30 days; annual cycle.

## Compliance hooks

CP-2, CP-2(1), CP-2(8), CP-3, CP-4, CP-4(1), CP-6, CP-6(1), CP-7,
CP-7(1), CP-7(3), CP-8, CP-8(1), CP-9, CP-10; AU-9 and IR-4 by
cross-reference. NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1; FISMA; OMB A-130. FedRAMP 20x
KSIs: backup and recovery; incident response and continuity.

## Prerequisites

Explicitly the whole series: DDI Grid replication (01), SD-WAN dual
underlay (02), break-glass identity (03, 07), SQL AG replicas (05–06),
config backups (08), compliance exports (09), geo-redundant Sentinel
logging (10). Facilitation and technical-writing skills matter as much as
engineering here.

## Labs

1. Conduct a mock BIA interview; produce a signed BIA row
   (MTD/RTO/RPO/WRT plus dependencies) for a sample system.
2. Run the book's 2-hour ransomware tabletop with its injects (absent
   CPC, wrong roster number, sync replica also compromised); complete the
   metrics table and AAR.
3. Script the quarterly device-policy export to a secondary-region vault
   and perform the annual CP-6 restore-and-integrity test.

## Pitfalls the book calls out

- Adjusting the MTD downward to match a convenient technical RTO — the
  MTD is a mission decision requiring mission-owner signature.
- Treating a wiki of runbooks as a Contingency Plan.
- A replica in the same region (AZ-only separation) fails CP-6(1)/CP-7(1)
  geographic separation.
- Clean test results are a red flag — a zero-finding tabletop signals an
  inadequate scenario. Keep personal phone numbers out of the plan body.
